opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core issue is that in a latent recurrent model the "thinking" happens entirely in a continuous hidden state. We iterate a recurrent block over and over, and the state just keeps evolving. You could look at that state directly and ask whether it has stopped changing, but that turns out to be a pretty awkward signal. The latent space is high-dimensional and not normalized in any meaningful way. Some directions matter a lot for the prediction, and many don't matter at all. A small change in the state might flip the answer, while a large change in some irrelevant subspace might do nothing. So a raw distance between successive states doesn't tell you much about whether the model is still doing useful work.

The next-token distribution, on the other hand, is exactly the quantity we actually care about. At the end of the day, the model has to commit to a token. If I decode the state after each recurrence step and the predicted distribution has essentially stopped moving, so the KL divergence between consecutive steps drops below some threshold, then more iterations aren't going to change what the model says. That's a very direct, task-relevant notion of convergence. It also has nice properties: it's a probability distribution, so it's comparable across tokens and across contexts, and you can set one threshold and have it behave sensibly everywhere.

What we found really interesting is that this naturally gives you per-token adaptive compute without training anything extra. Easy tokens, like finishing a common word or some punctuation, converge in just a few steps. Harder tokens, say in the middle of a math problem or when the model has to retrieve a fact, keep shifting for much longer before they settle. So the model kind of tells you on its own how hard each step is, and you don't need a separate halting head or a learned ponder cost like in some of the older adaptive computation work, which were often finicky to train.

There are caveats, of course. A distribution can plateau temporarily and then move again, and there are cases where the model sits in a sort of orbit in latent space rather than converging to a fixed point. But even then, if the output distribution is stable, that's usually a good sign that you can stop. So overall it's just the most honest proxy we have for "has the model finished thinking about this token."

r001.rationale: The response proposes stopping when the KL divergence between consecutive steps’ next-token distributions drops below a threshold.

r002.rationale: It explains that latent-state changes in irrelevant subspaces may have no effect on the next-token prediction.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the basic question is: the model is iterating this recurrent block in latent space, and at some point you have to decide to stop and actually produce a token. And the obvious thing to try is to look at the latent state itself, right? You could say, if the hidden state stops changing much between iterations, we've converged, we're done. And we did look at that. The problem is that the latent state is this high-dimensional object that we don't really have a good handle on. It can keep drifting in directions that don't matter at all for what the model is about to say, or conversely it can look fairly stable while the decision at the output is still actually flipping. So a norm on the hidden state difference is kind of measuring the wrong thing.

Whereas the next-token distribution is exactly the thing we care about. That's the quantity that's going to be consumed downstream. So if you take the output distribution at step r and at step r plus one and look at the KL divergence between them, and that's very small, then by definition additional compute isn't changing what the model would do. It's a very direct criterion. And it's cheap, because you already have the output head, you're just applying it at intermediate steps instead of only at the end.

The other thing I like about it is that it's interpretable, in the sense that it gives you an actual per-token picture of where the model is spending effort. You see, you know, a token that's just completing a word, the distribution locks in after a couple of iterations and you stop. And then you hit a token that requires some actual decision, and the distribution keeps moving for many more steps before it settles. That's really the behavior you want from adaptive compute, and you get it for free from the training, without ever having explicitly trained the model to exit early. We trained with a random number of recurrences, so the model learned to produce something reasonable at any depth, and this criterion just reads off when it has effectively made up its mind.

I'd add one caveat, which is that convergence in the output distribution is not the same as correctness. The model can be confidently wrong early and stay wrong. So it's a stopping signal, not a verification signal. But as a stopping signal, it's about as close as you can get to measuring the thing you actually want to measure.

r001.rationale: The response proposes stopping when the KL divergence between the next-token distributions at recurrent steps r and r+1 is very small.

r002.rationale: It says the latent state can keep drifting in directions that do not matter for the output, so continued latent changes need not change the next-token distribution.

astra-6.text:
Because what we ultimately care about is whether another step of computation changes the prediction. The latent state can keep moving around without meaningfully changing what the model would say next, so measuring how much that state changes is a somewhat indirect signal.

If you look at the next-token distribution across recurrent steps, you can ask: is the model still revising its answer, or has that distribution stabilized? If it’s still changing, there’s a reason to keep computing. If it’s essentially the same, another step may not buy you much.

And that’s different from just asking whether the model is confident. You can have a stable distribution that’s uncertain because there are several reasonable next tokens. More thinking doesn’t necessarily resolve that uncertainty. So the useful signal is whether additional computation is still affecting the prediction, rather than whether the model has become maximally confident.

r001.rationale: The response says to stop when the next-token distribution is essentially unchanged, but it does not specify KL divergence as the measure between distributions at recurrent steps.

r002.rationale: The response says the latent state can keep moving without meaningfully changing what the model predicts next.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, what we really care about is whether more computation is going to change the answer. The hidden state can keep moving around, but that doesn’t necessarily mean the model is making progress in a way that matters for its prediction. It might just be changing aspects of the representation that don’t affect the output.

So looking at the next-token distribution gives us a signal that’s directly tied to the task. If that distribution is still changing across recurrent steps, there’s a reason to keep going. If it has stabilized, then additional steps may not be buying us much, even if the hidden state hasn’t converged.

And that’s different from just asking whether the model is confident. You can have a stable distribution that’s uncertain because the next token is genuinely ambiguous. The question is whether more thinking is changing that uncertainty. It’s not a guarantee that the answer is correct, but it’s a more direct way to ask whether another step of computation is useful.

r001.rationale: The response says to stop when the next-token distribution has stabilized, but it does not specify KL divergence between distributions at different steps.

r002.rationale: It explicitly observes that the hidden state can keep changing without affecting the model’s output distribution.
